latin.402: GAR. Respondeo. Voluntatem Adae fuisse voluntatem omnium, satis tritum est apud Theologos, neque Augustino ignoratum. Per unius enim Adami voluntatem malam omnes in eo peccaverunt, quando omnes ille unus fuerunt, inquit de Nupt. & Concup. lib. 1. cap. 5. Et tamen hoc dictum non modo tanquam dubium, aut improbabile, aut falsum vir doctus exagitat; verum etiam, tanquam ineptum & fatuum, & anilium fabularum nugamenta superans, traducit, atque subsannat. PLAC. Negavi, praeeunte Chamiero praestanti Theologo, Adami voluntatem fuisse nostram voluntatem, & quae, si dicatur fuisse nostra voluntas, sequantur absurda, absque ullo asperiore verbo, ostendi. Fecine ea in re quicquam praeter officium meum? At voluntatem Adae fuisse voluntatem omnium satis tritum est apud Theologos. Quaeso, apud quos? Eorum certe autoritas non impedivit, quominus Chamierus, & ipse, opinor, Theologus, id negaret. Cur mihi quoque id negare non licuit? Opponitur mihi Augustinus, qui tamen totus meus est.
latin.403: Dixitne voluntatem Adami fuisse voluntatem omnium? Non, sed per unius illius voluntatem malam omnes in eo peccasse, quando omnes ille (malim ille) unus fuerunt, de quo propterea singuli peccatum originale traxerunt. Quando autem unus fuerunt? nimirum quando ipsi non fuerunt, sed unus fuit unde suum esse traxerunt. Quomodo in eo tunc peccaverunt? nimirum ipsi tunc non peccaverunt, sed ille peccavit cuius ex peccato suum singuli peccatum originale traxerunt. Id autem peccatum, non per voluntatem omnium, sed per voluntatem unius illius commissum est. Cum ergo dicit fuisse voluntatem unius illius, non affirmat, sed negat potius fuisse voluntatem omnium. At dicit omnes fuisse illum unum, nempe quando ille unus fuit, & ipsi non fuerunt. Simul enim ac ipsi esse coeperunt, non fuerunt amplius unus, sed ab eo uno diversi: id quod arguit vox quando: innuit enim quo tempore loquebatur, eos non esse amplius unum. Si ex quo sumus, non sumus unus ille homo, certe ex quo sumus eius voluntas non est nostra voluntas, nec ad eam similem habemus relationem ei quam habent membra ad voluntatem totius hominis, ut verbis Thomae asseverabaris cum quo disputabam. Mihi igitur favet potius Augustinus quam nocet.
latin.404: Vis scire quomodo per voluntatem unius peccavimus? Ex voluntate, inquit, peccatum est. Quaerit forte etiam & originale peccatum. Respondeo prorsus originale peccatum, quia & hoc ex voluntate primi hominis seminatum est, ut & in illo esset, & in omnes transiret. Putavitne cum viro docto id per imputationem transire, & huius causam unicam esse Dei voluntatem? Contra plane; contendit neque Deo, neque naturae humanae ut est a Deo, sed concupiscentiae seu libidini quae a parente in liberos transit per semen debere ascribi. Non vult immediate ab Adamo per imputationem vitium descendere, sed mediate, & a proximi cuiusque parentis vitio per carnalem generationem trajici in prolem. Cumque inquirat, quomodo quod dimissum est in parente trahatur in prolem, id quidem miris modis fieri dicit, sed tamen fieri: & illustrat exemplo olivae ex qua nascitur oleaster. Si idem cum viro docto sensisset, non confugisset ad naturam, non ad carnalem generationem, non ad vitium proximorum parentum, non ad oleastri exemplum, sed ad voluntatem Dei, cui placuit omnibus Adami posteris peccatum actuale immediate imputare, & ut illud imputatum puniret, & satisfaceret justitiae, ipsis omnibus vitium illud originale infligere. Aliter enim illius rei rationem reddi non posse clamat vir doctus multis locis, ac nominatim cap. 11. §. 8. de quo supra pag. 125.
latin.405: GAR. Videamus tamen, an ista colligendi ratio, ut jocularis argutiola laudem habere potest, ita soliditatis habeat. Etenim respondeo, eam Adami voluntatem, de qua loquimur, & singularem fuisse, & universalem. Singularem actus proprietate; universalem repraesentationis jure. Singularem, quia ab uno ex individuis humanis profecta est: universalem, quia individuum illud repraesentavit universum genus, ut eo per voluntatem suam primum peccante, idem fuerit, ac si omnes per propriam suam voluntatem peccassent. 2. Voluntatem Adae cum dicimus fuisse voluntatem omnium, non loquimur de voluntate prout significat facultatem illam volendi, quae Adamo ex naturae principiis inerat, & sine qua ne homo quidem fuisset: sed voluntatis nomine intelligimus volitionem, sive actum illum volendi quem exercuit circa fructum arboris vetitae, & quo se reum fecit inobedientiae illius primae. Neque dicimus actum illum volendi fuisse omnium proprie, formaliter, aut personaliter, sed interpretative & per imputationem. Itaque quae inde nectuntur conclusiunculae, Adami animam, corpus, uxorem fuisse nostra; nos habere duas voluntates, animas, corpora, & esse duos homines, eo loco possit habere aliquis, quo haberi voluit vir doctus illud Theologorum effatum.
latin.406: PLAC. Ergo, si fides habetur viro docto, cum voluntas Adami dicitur voluntas omnium, nihil aliud significatur, nisi volitionem illam qua primum peccavit, hoc est, primam eius inobedientiam esse omnium per imputationem: id quod toto hoc libro refellimus. Sed quo jure est omnium? Est, inquit, universalis repraesentationis jure. Estne igitur, ut loquuntur, universalis in repraesentando? Non, opinor, hoc voluit. Quid ergo voluit? nam quo fuit voluntas omnium, eo fuit voluntas universalis; universale enim & commune idem videntur significare. Fuit autem, si illi creditur, omnium imputatione. Probabilius est eum intellexisse jus repraesentationis, quo scilicet Adamus repraesentavit omnes homines. At si repraesentavit omnes homines, potuit non minus quam sua voluntas, dici homo universalis: quo tamen elogio nondum, ut opinor, a quoquam est insignitus. Deinde merito quaeri potest, quo fundamento istiusmodi repraesentatio, & repraesentationis jus nitatur. Proferetur fortasse foedus illud initum cum toto genere humano in Adamo, quod ad imputationem immediatam tuendam viri quidam docti praeter Scripturam & naturam excogitarunt: Sed de eo & jam dictum est, & nihil necesse est nunc disputare. Haec enim obiter hoc loco observare volui: redeo ad id de quo agebatur in Manuscripto, & quod mihi videtur vir doctus hac sua responsione detorsisse in alienum sensum. Patet enim ex verbis Thomae, quibus suam mentem is vir doctus, quicum mihi res erat, exposuit, per voluntatem, non ipsam volitionem, sed volitionis principium intelligi, sicut per membra, non actiones membrorum, sed harum principia significantur. Considerantur enim a Thoma omnes homines tanquam partes seu membra naturae humanae, & voluntas Adami ut voluntas totius naturae, vel, ut loquitur, principii naturae humanae: quae comparatio flagitat, ut quemadmodum membra non significant actiones membrorum, sed illarum principia, sic voluntas non significet actionem voluntatis, sed eius principium.
latin.407: GAR. Quid si accedat aliquis de Socini schola, & arma mutuatus a viro docto similibus conclusionum tormentis agat adversus id quod habet Gallica S. Coenae liturgia, virtutem mortis Christi ad justitiam nobis imputari, non minus quam si eam nos ipsi pertulissemus? Si actus ille voluntatis Christi, quo se in mortem obtulit, tam tuus est, quam si tu actu proprio voluntatis tuae teipsum obtulisses, quiani etiam tua fuerit anima, corpus, mater Christi? Quidni duas voluntates habere dicaris, unam antequam esses, alteram postquam fuisti? &c. PLAC. Dixitne liturgia illa, voluntatem Christi fuisse voluntatem omnium nostrum? Aut actum illum voluntatis Christi, quo se in mortem obtulit, fuisse actum omnium nostrum? Minime: dixit tantum, virtutem mortis Christi ad justitiam nobis imputari. Aliud autem est virtus mortis Christi, aliud voluntas Christi. Nihil igitur video in verbis liturgiae unde tales consequentiae deduci possint. Cur autem virtus mortis Christi nobis imputatur? Annon quia mortem luere tenebamur, ille, ut vas noster, eam loco nostro luit? Itaque nostra est Dei & Christi donatione, nostraque per fidem acceptione. Num similiter Adamus vas noster fuit, ut loco nostro peccaret? Aut eius peccatum factum est dono Dei, & Adami, & nostra acceptione, nostrum?

pass_a.402: GAR answers that Adam's will as the will of all is common among theologians and known to Augustine (De Nupt. 1.5: by one bad will all sinned in him when all were that one). He says Placeus assails this as doubtful, false, even fatuous. Placeus: with Chamier he denied Adam's will was ours and showed the absurdities without harsh words—his duty. "Worn among theologians"—among whom? Their authority did not stop Chamier from denying it; why may Placeus not? Augustine is opposed, yet wholly Placeus's.
pass_a.403: Placeus: Augustine did not say Adam's will was everyone's will, but that by that one's bad will all sinned in him when they were that one—namely when they themselves were not yet, and one was from whom they drew their being. They themselves did not then sin; he sinned, and from his sin each drew his own original sin—committed through that one's will, not through the will of all. Saying it was that one's will rather denies it was everyone's. The word "when" proves that once they began to be they were no longer one but diverse from him. From the time we are, we are not that one man, so his will is not ours, nor have we to it a relation like members to the whole man's will as asserted from Thomas. Therefore Augustine favors Placeus rather than hurts him.
pass_a.404: Augustine: from the will there is sin, including original sin sown from the first man's will to be in him and pass into all. He does not think with the learned man that it passes by immediate imputation from God's will alone; he ascribes it to concupiscence or lust passing by seed from parent to children—mediately from each nearest parent's vice by carnal generation, illustrated by the olive from which a wild olive is born. Had he agreed with the learned man he would have fled to God's will pleased immediately to impute Adam's actual sin to all posterity and inflict original vice to punish it and satisfy justice—which the learned man cries (cap. 11 §8, p. 125) is the only account that can be given.
pass_a.405: GAR presses whether Placeus's gathering has solidity or only joking quibble. Adam's will was singular by the act's property and universal by right of representation—one human individual representing the whole race so that when he first sinned by his will it was as if all had sinned by their own. "Will of all" does not mean the faculty of willing without which he would not be man, but the volition about the forbidden fruit by which he became guilty of first disobedience—not properly, formally, or personally everyone's, but interpretatively and by imputation. So Placeus's little conclusions (Adam's soul, body, wife ours; two wills, souls, bodies; two men) may be put where the learned man wanted the theologians' saying held.
pass_a.406: Placeus: if the learned man is credited, when Adam's will is called the will of all, nothing else is meant than that the volition by which he first sinned—his first disobedience—is everyone's by imputation, which this whole book refutes. By what right is it everyone's? He says universal by right of representation. Is it then universal in representing? Placeus doubts that was meant; insofar as it was the will of all it would be a universal will, yet if credited it is everyone's by imputation. More probably he meant the right by which Adam represented all men—which would let Adam no less than his will be called a universal man, an elogium Placeus thinks no one has yet given. Next: on what foundation do such representation and right rest? Perhaps the covenant entered with the whole race in Adam, invented by certain learned men beyond Scripture and nature to guard immediate imputation—already treated; no need to dispute now. These notes in passing; returning to the Manuscript, the learned man seems to have twisted Thomas into an alien sense. From Thomas's words by which that opponent expounded his mind, will means not the volition itself but the principle of volition—as members signify not actions but their principles—and Adam's will is considered the will of the whole nature or of the principle of human nature, which comparison demands that will not signify the act of will but its principle.
pass_a.407: GAR: someone from Socinus's school could borrow Placeus's engines against the French Lord's Supper liturgy—that the virtue of Christ's death is imputed unto righteousness as if we ourselves bore it—asking if Christ's offering-will is yours, why not also his soul, body, and mother, and why not two wills before and after you were. Placeus: the liturgy never said Christ's will or that offering-act was the act of us all—only that the virtue of his death is imputed unto righteousness. Virtue of death is one thing, Christ's will another; no such consequences follow. Why imputed? Because we owed death and he as our surety paid it in our place—ours by God's and Christ's gift and by acceptance through faith. Was Adam likewise our surety so as to sin in our place, or did his sin become ours by gift and our acceptance? Tip before further assertion on Adam's will.

402: GAR. I answer. That Adam's will was the will of all is worn enough among Theologians, and not unknown to Augustine. For by the one Adam's bad will all sinned in him, when all were that one, he says in De Nuptiis et Concupiscentia book 1 chapter 5. And yet the learned man assails this saying not only as doubtful or improbable or false, but even traduces and scoffs at it as inept and fatuous and surpassing old wives' fables. PLAC. I denied, with the excellent theologian Chamier going before, that Adam's will was our will, and without any harsher word I showed what absurdities follow if it is said to have been our will. Did I do anything in that beyond my duty? But that Adam's will was the will of all is worn enough among Theologians. Among whom, I ask? Their authority certainly did not keep Chamier—himself a theologian, I think—from denying it. Why may I not deny it too? Augustine is opposed to me—who yet is wholly mine.
403: Did he say Adam's will was the will of all? No—but that by that one's bad will all sinned in him when all were that one (I prefer "he"), from whom therefore each drew original sin. When were they one? Namely when they themselves were not, but one was from whom they drew their being. How did they then sin in him? Namely they themselves did not then sin, but he sinned from whose sin each drew his own original sin. And that sin was committed not through the will of all, but through that one's will. So when he says it was that one's will, he does not affirm but rather denies it was the will of all. Yet he says all were that one—namely when he was one and they were not. For as soon as they began to be, they were no longer one, but diverse from that one: which the word "when" proves; it hints that at the time he was speaking they were no longer one. If from the time we are we are not that one man, then from the time we are his will is not our will, nor have we to it a relation like that which members have to the whole man's will, as you were asserting in Thomas's words with whom I disputed. So Augustine favors me rather than hurts me.
404: Do you want to know how we sinned through one will? From the will, he says, there is sin. Perhaps he seeks original sin too. I answer: original sin altogether, because this too was sown from the first man's will so that it might be in him and pass into all. Did he think with the learned man that it passes by imputation, and that its sole cause is God's will? Plainly the contrary; he contends it should be ascribed neither to God nor to human nature as from God, but to concupiscence or lust which passes from parent to children through seed. He does not want the vice to descend immediately from Adam by imputation, but mediately, and to be carried into the offspring from each nearest parent's vice by carnal generation. And when he asks how what is remitted in the parent is drawn into the offspring, he says it happens in wondrous ways, yet happens—and illustrates with the olive from which a wild olive is born. Had he sensed with the learned man, he would not have fled to nature, carnal generation, nearest parents' vice, or the wild-olive example, but to God's will, which was pleased immediately to impute Adam's actual sin to all his posterity and, to punish that imputed sin and satisfy justice, to inflict that original vice on them all. For otherwise, the learned man cries in many places—and namely cap. 11 §8, above at p. 125—no account of the matter can be given.
405: GAR. Yet let us see whether that way of gathering, as it can have praise as a joking quibble, so has solidity. For I answer that that will of Adam of which we speak was both singular and universal: singular by the property of the act; universal by right of representation. Singular, because it proceeded from one of the human individuals; universal, because that individual represented the whole race, so that when he first sinned by his will it was the same as if all had sinned by their own proper will. 2. When we say Adam's will was the will of all, we do not speak of will as signifying that faculty of willing which was in Adam from nature's principles and without which he would not even have been a man: but by the name of will we understand volition, or that act of willing which he exercised about the fruit of the forbidden tree and by which he made himself guilty of that first disobedience. Nor do we say that act of willing was everyone's properly, formally, or personally, but interpretatively and by imputation. So the little conclusions thence woven—that Adam's soul, body, wife were ours; that we have two wills, souls, bodies, and are two men—someone may put in the place where the learned man wanted the Theologians' saying held.
406: PLAC. Therefore, if the learned man is credited, when Adam's will is called the will of all, nothing else is meant than that the volition by which he first sinned—that is, his first disobedience—is everyone's by imputation: which this whole book refutes. But by what right is it everyone's? It is, he says, universal by right of representation. Is it then, as they say, universal in representing? I do not think he meant that. What then did he mean?—for insofar as it was the will of all, it was a universal will; universal and common seem to signify the same. Yet if he is believed, it was everyone's by imputation. More probably he meant the right of representation by which Adam represented all men. But if he represented all men, he could no less than his will be called a universal man—an elogium with which, I think, no one has yet marked him. Next it may fairly be asked on what foundation such representation and right of representation rest. Perhaps that covenant entered with the whole human race in Adam will be brought forward, which certain learned men invented beyond Scripture and nature to guard immediate imputation: but of that enough has already been said, and there is no need to dispute now. These things I wished to note in passing here: I return to what was treated in the Manuscript, and what the learned man seems to me by this reply to have twisted into an alien sense. For it is clear from Thomas's words, by which that learned man with whom I had to do expounded his mind, that by will not the volition itself but the principle of volition is understood, just as by members not the members' actions but their principles are signified. For Thomas considers all men as parts or members of human nature, and Adam's will as the will of the whole nature, or, as he speaks, of the principle of human nature: which comparison demands that as members do not signify the members' actions but their principles, so will not signify the act of will but its principle.
407: GAR. What if someone from Socinus's school should come, and borrowing arms from the learned man should with like engines of conclusions fight against what the French Lord's Supper liturgy has—that the virtue of Christ's death is imputed to us unto righteousness, no less than if we ourselves had borne it? If that act of Christ's will by which he offered himself unto death is as much yours as if by your own act of will you had offered yourself, why then was not Christ's soul, body, mother also yours? Why not be said to have two wills—one before you were, another after you had been? &c. PLAC. Did that liturgy say Christ's will was the will of us all? Or that that act of Christ's will by which he offered himself unto death was an act of us all? Not at all: it said only that the virtue of Christ's death is imputed to us unto righteousness. But the virtue of Christ's death is one thing, Christ's will another. So I see nothing in the liturgy's words from which such consequences can be drawn. Why then is the virtue of Christ's death imputed to us? Is it not because we were bound to pay death, and he, as our surety, paid it in our place? So it is ours by God's and Christ's gift, and ours by acceptance through faith. Was Adam likewise our surety so as to sin in our place? Or did his sin become ours by gift of God and of Adam and by our acceptance?
